articles.summary: A neutral comparison of LIHE Precision with machine-maker (OEM) suppliers such as Husky, SACMI, SIPA and Sidel for PET cap molds, blow molds and tooling retrofits, using only published data, with fit criteria and steps to start a project.

sections.heading: Short answer: how does LIHE compare with OEM suppliers?
paragraphs: An OEM supplier is a company that supplies tooling for the machines it builds itself.

LIHE is an independent tooling maker that supplies cap molds, blow molds and retrofits for several machine brands, while OEM suppliers such as Husky, SACMI, SIPA and Sidel build tooling around their own machines and publish proprietary features and service programs. LIHE publishes concrete lead times (4 weeks for cap mold parts, 8 weeks for standard PET molds) and a retrofit cost of 25%–40% of a new mold price; OEMs publish platform-specific figures such as Husky's HyCAP 4.0 target of more than 50 million cycles of stack life. Neither side publishes prices on the pages cited here.

LIHE Precision (Foshan Lihe Precision Machinery Co.,Ltd.) is a manufacturer of PET preform molds, blow molds, closure and compression molds, hot runner systems and mold components for the beverage and packaging industry, with manufacturing in Foshan, China.
Disclosure: this article is published by LIHE. OEM information comes only from the official web pages listed under References. LIHE is not affiliated with any machine maker named here.

sections.heading: What LIHE offers in the three categories
list: Cap molds: closure injection molds from 12 to 72 cavities for one-piece and two-piece caps, tamper-evident bands and EU tethered caps, in 26mm, 28mm, 2925, 3025 and 38mm.
Compression molds: tooling for SACMI CCM lines, including replacement tooling made from existing parts.
Blow molds for two-step machines: SIDEL, KRONES, SIG/KHS, TECH-LONG and NEWAMSTAR, including KHS InnoPET Blomax and Krones Contiform cold fill sets.
Blow molds for one-step machines: SIPA, ASB and AOKI.
Blow mold applications: cold fill, hot fill at about 85–95°C and aseptic, plus split-type quick-change molds and water bottles of 330ml, 500ml, 550ml and 1.5L.

Retrofits: complete mold overhauls and performance upgrades to restore aging assets to OEM-level efficiency, neck finish conversions, lightweighting of 1g to 2g and cooling optimization that can cut neck cooling time by up to 0.5 seconds.

articles.title: What are the risks of switching PET mold suppliers in the middle of a beverage packaging project?
articles.summary: Control a PET mold supplier change through an approved design baseline, verified interfaces, transferred trial evidence and a clear acceptance plan.

heroImage.alt: Illustrative controlled handover of PET preform molds and samples

detailImage.alt: Illustrative metrology inspection of replacement mold inserts

sections.heading: The main risk is losing the approved technical baseline
paragraphs: A mid-project supplier switch is a change of mold supplier after design, steel or trial work has already started.

A supplier handover is the transfer of a defined tooling scope and its approved technical information to another manufacturer. The principal risks are mismatched drawing revisions, incomplete machine interfaces, lost trial evidence, unclear responsibility and a production schedule built on unconfirmed assumptions. A switch can be managed, but the new supplier must qualify the actual remaining work instead of treating the project as an unchanged repeat order.

sections.heading: Transfer the evidence that the next manufacturer will need
list: Collect the current approved drawings and a record of changes already agreed. Separate drawings released for manufacture from working drafts. Identify outstanding design decisions and the person authorized to close them, so the new supplier does not manufacture from a superseded file.

Provide the actual machine configuration and list the tooling assemblies already built or installed. Preserve measurements of unresolved interfaces and document any deviation accepted earlier. A replacement manufacturer needs the configuration that will operate, not only the original project proposal.

Transfer identified trial samples, inspection reports, resin information, process settings and defect records. Include failed trials and corrective actions alongside successful samples. Without the unsuccessful evidence, the next supplier can repeat an earlier problem while appearing to follow the approved design.

Confirm which documents and parts are available for authorized use. Resolve missing technical information through agreed measurements or an interface audit. Do not assume that changing suppliers provides access to the previous manufacturer’s proprietary design files.

sections.heading: Decide whether to switch before the remaining work grows
list: If manufacture has not started, the main task is to align the revised specification and responsibilities. If parts are already machined, first inspect what exists and define what the next manufacturer can retain. The later stage needs a condition-based handover rather than an assumption that all work is reusable.

For a mixed assembly, assign responsibility for the old-to-new interface. The new supplier should identify what it will inspect and what it accepts as customer-supplied equipment. Keep the complete mold acceptance separate from inspection of the newly supplied parts.

Revise the production plan to include engineering review, trials and corrective work. LIHE’s published lead times below are product information, not confirmation that a partly completed handover will meet the same schedule. Confirm a project-specific timeline after reviewing the transfer package.

LIHE publishes tooling conversion and support services, making it a candidate for a defined replacement scope. That does not establish the condition of unfinished components or transfer another supplier’s obligations. Choose the switch only after the remaining work, acceptance plan and fallback production route are clear.

sections.heading: Acceptance at the point of handover
paragraphs: A mid-project switch needs two acceptances, not one: acceptance of what is handed over, and acceptance of the finished tool. Treating the second as sufficient leaves nobody responsible for parts that were faulty when they changed hands.
steps: Hold a joint inspection before the previous supplier’s work is formally closed. Record every finished or half-finished component with its drawing revision and measured condition, and have the buyer and both suppliers sign the inventory.

Give the new supplier a defined period to inspect the transferred parts and either accept them as customer-supplied items or reject them with a written reason. Parts accepted at this stage become part of the new supplier’s integration responsibility.

Repeat at least one trial that the previous supplier already ran, using the same resin, machine and settings. Matching the earlier results shows that the technical baseline transferred correctly before any new change is introduced.

Qualify the mixed tool as a whole: preforms measured by cavity, finished bottles and an agreed production run. A pass on the newly supplied components alone does not prove that their interfaces with retained parts work.

Close the handover with a single document set: the drawing revision that now applies, the current parts list, process settings and a list of open items with an owner. Archive the previous supplier’s documents separately so that they are not reused by mistake.

sections.heading: Keep maintenance and spares continuous across the switch
list: Map every spare part the plant holds to its supplier and drawing number. After the switch, some spares may no longer fit the revised tool; label them clearly before someone installs one by mistake during a breakdown.

Decide who maintains the parts still made by the previous supplier, for example an existing hot runner. If that supplier will no longer service them, ask the new supplier to quote refurbishment or replacement before the first failure occurs.
Ask the new supplier for its part numbering and a cross-reference to the previous numbers. A dual list kept during the transition period prevents wrong orders and duplicated stock.

Agree the date of the first on-site visit for installation and start-up, and what remote troubleshooting covers until then. Note what local staff must measure or photograph so that remote diagnosis is actually possible.

Keep the previously approved mold, if one exists, in running condition until the replacement has passed site acceptance. It is the plant’s only fallback if the new tool needs correction after delivery.

sections.heading: What LIHE publishes about taking over a tooling project
paragraphs: LIHE Precision wrote this guide and may itself be the supplier a buyer is switching to, which is worth keeping in mind while reading it. Only the published items that matter for a handover are listed here; each of them appears on lihe-preform.com.
list: Conversion parts: published as 100% interchangeable with Husky, SACMI, SIPA, NETSTAL, MHT, OTTO, ASB, Krupps and Corvaglia systems, and replacement parts can be made from a customer’s existing Husky, SACMI or Otto parts. Confirm interchangeability on the actual parts being transferred.
Engineering: CAD/CAM, 3D simulation and flow analysis before production, which can help rebuild a design baseline when the transferred drawings are incomplete.
Measurement: an in-house Zeiss CMM lab, with inspection reports supplied on request, which is relevant when transferred parts have to be measured at the handover.
Preform molds: 32 to 160 cavities for HUSKY, NETSTAL, SIPA, KATA and other machines, so the takeover of a typical preform project falls within the published range.

Published lead times run from 20 days (pilot molds) through 4 weeks (replacement parts) to 8 weeks (standard PET molds). In a handover these are starting points only; the real schedule depends on what is transferred and in what condition.
After-sales: on-site machine interface audits, mold installation, start-up support, remote troubleshooting and refurbishment programs.

faq.question: Is switching suppliers always the wrong choice?
faq.answer: No. The decision depends on the actual remaining scope and the evidence available for a controlled handover. Establish what can be retained and what must be requalified before committing.

faq.question: Can the new supplier use the previous trial results?
faq.answer: They are useful if linked to identified drawings, resin, samples and settings. The new or mixed assembly still needs the agreed acceptance checks; previous evidence does not automatically qualify changed components.

faq.question: What should happen to unfinished parts?
faq.answer: Inspect and identify them before defining reuse. Record drawing revision, dimensions and condition, then agree which parts the new supplier accepts and which require correction or replacement.

faq.question: How should the plant protect production?
faq.answer: Maintain an approved existing tool or another agreed production route until the replacement qualifies. Plan the change around acceptance readiness, not merely the arrival of the new mold.

articles.title: How much should I expect to pay for a PET bottle mold retrofit or lightweighting project?
articles.summary: Define the retrofit boundary, retained-tool condition and package tests before requesting a lightweighting quotation and using a published cost comparison.

heroImage.alt: Illustrative PET mold refurbishment and lightweighting inspection bench

detailImage.alt: Illustrative replacement neck rings and cores beside preforms and bottles

sections.heading: Use the published comparison only for a suitable defined retrofit
paragraphs: A mold retrofit is a rebuild of an existing mold in which selected parts are replaced or modified instead of buying a new tool.

A mold retrofit is a modification of existing tooling, while lightweighting changes the package design to reduce material use without abandoning the approved performance requirements. LIHE publishes that lightweighting retrofits cost 25%–40% of a new mold price, but an exact price for your project requires an inspection and a scope-specific quotation. That published ratio is not a universal market price and does not apply automatically to every bottle blow mold or preform conversion.

sections.heading: Separate the changes hidden inside a lightweighting brief

head: Project element
Possible tooling boundary
What must be confirmed
rows: Neck rings and related conversion parts
Blow mold and possibly format parts

sections.heading: Inspect the existing asset before calculating the project scope
list: Provide the current mold drawings, service history, known modifications and representative samples. Identify the defect or design change that triggered the project. A retrofit intended to reduce weight is a different task from repairing wear or restoring an unstable process, even when the same mold is involved.

Ask the supplier to identify which assemblies remain usable and which must change. Include the condition of the mold base, shaping components, cooling circuits and hot runner where relevant. Do not assume that a new set of inserts corrects every problem in the retained equipment.

Clarify whether the quotation covers preform injection tooling, bottle blow tooling or both. The preform determines material distribution during blowing, but the bottle body is formed in separate blow tooling on a two-step line. A project name such as “bottle lightweighting” does not identify the actual bill of supply.

Agree what happens if inspection reveals a wider replacement requirement. The commercial proposal should distinguish the confirmed work from unresolved condition-dependent items, so the plant can decide whether the retrofit remains technically and operationally suitable.

sections.heading: Evaluate the saving with package and production evidence
list: Use LIHE’s published weight-reduction proposals as a discussion of achievable design scope, not an unconditional promise for the current bottle. The target must retain the required neck, closure and bottle performance. Record any changes needed to the blowing process and handling parts.

Base material savings on the approved actual weight change and accepted production volume. Keep resin consumption, startup scrap and rejected bottles visible. No payback period is calculated here because the plant’s resin costs, output, downtime and project quotation have not been supplied.

Compare a technically suitable retrofit with a technically suitable new tool under the same package requirements. Include trial work, spare parts and commissioning. The published percentage can start a discussion, but it cannot establish equivalent scope between two incomplete quotations.

LIHE’s offering includes mold overhauls, lightweighting and line conversions. This does not establish the condition of your existing asset or guarantee the finished bottle. Approve the project on inspection findings, agreed drawings and package tests before changing the production tool.

sections.heading: Reading a retrofit offer against the 25%–40% figure
list: LIHE’s published figure is that a lightweighting retrofit of an existing mold costs 25%–40% of the price of a new mold. Use it as a plausibility check on a retrofit offer, and only after the supplier has confirmed in writing that the existing mold is fit for reuse.

Ask for the retrofit offer to show retained parts and replaced parts in two separate columns, for example mold base and hot runner retained, cores and neck rings new. Without that split the percentage cannot be related to any physical scope.

Request a reference offer for the equivalent new mold from the same supplier, built to the same preform drawing and for the same machine. The ratio only means something when both offers describe the same finished preform and the same acceptance terms.

Show refurbishment of the retained parts separately from the lightweighting change itself. Worn guide elements, leaking cooling circuits or a hot runner that needs servicing add cost that belongs to maintenance, not to the weight reduction, and should be budgeted as such.

List the costs that sit outside the mold: trial resin, blow-mold or format-part adjustments, line downtime for the change-over and requalification of the bottle. They do not appear in the mold percentage, yet they decide whether the project actually pays back.

sections.heading: Material and package checks that a lighter preform triggers
list: Removing 1 g to 2 g from a preform leaves less material to stretch into the same bottle. Ask the bottle designer to confirm that wall thickness at the shoulder, panel and base still meets the package specification before any steel is cut.

If the project also introduces recycled PET (rPET), run the lighter design and the new resin as separate trial steps. Changing both at once makes it impossible to tell whether a later defect comes from the geometry or from the material.

Dry the resin according to the resin producer’s instructions and log the lot number of every trial run. Thinner walls can make moisture- or temperature-related defects more visible, so keep the drying record together with the samples.

When the neck is part of the change, involve the closure supplier from the start. A shorter neck or a different finish, such as PCO 1881 or 29/25, must still seal and pass capping and torque checks with the closures the plant actually buys.

Food-contact and regulatory documentation belongs to the resin and packaging owners, not to the mold maker. Prepare that paperwork in parallel with the tooling work so that it does not hold up a retrofit that has otherwise passed its trials.

sections.heading: Accepting a retrofitted mold in stages
steps: Before any steel is removed, measure the existing mold and keep reference preforms from every cavity. This baseline shows exactly what the retrofit changed and protects both sides if the retained parts later develop problems.

Approve the new preform drawing and the list of parts to be changed in writing. Mark which dimensions are expected to move and which, such as the neck interface with the closure, must remain identical to the baseline.

Run the retrofitted tool and record the new preform weight per cavity against the baseline values. Accept the weight reduction only when it is consistent across all cavities, not as an average over the whole mold.

Blow the lighter preforms on the plant’s blow molder, or an equivalent machine, and test the bottles against the package specification. Keep the bottles that fail; they show where the material distribution needs further adjustment.

After reinstallation, run a production lot long enough to reveal scrap and stoppage rates, and compare them with the baseline mold. Close the retrofit only when the lighter preform runs at a reject level the plant has agreed in advance.

sections.heading: LIHE retrofit services and the figures behind them
paragraphs: LIHE Precision publishes this article and sells retrofit and lightweighting work itself, so its figures should be read as a supplier’s own statements rather than independent data. The points below are published on lihe-preform.com and are the ones that bear on a retrofit budget.
list: Retrofit cost: LIHE states that lightweighting retrofits of existing molds cost 25%–40% of a new mold price and describes the payback period as short. The payback a particular plant achieves depends on its own resin price, volumes and downtime.
Weight reduction: LIHE’s lightweighting proposals reduce preform weight by 1 g to 2 g through neck or wall-thickness optimization.
Cooling: LIHE says a reworked cooling layout can cut the neck’s cooling time by as much as 0.5 seconds. Treat this as an upper bound and confirm the effect on your own tool during the trial.
Scope of work: complete mold overhauls, neck-finish conversions, rPET material trials and replacement parts made from customers’ existing Husky, SACMI or Otto parts.
Timing: replacement parts are published with a 4-week lead time. Agree separately how long the mold will be out of production, including trials and reinstallation.

faq.question: Is the published retrofit ratio a fixed quotation?
faq.answer: No. It is LIHE’s published comparison for lightweighting retrofits. Confirm the existing mold’s condition, the retained assemblies and the equivalent new-tool scope before using it in a project evaluation.

faq.question: Does every lightweighting project need new blow molds?
faq.answer: Not automatically. The preform, bottle design and machine interfaces determine what changes. The supplier must identify the affected injection tooling, blow tooling and format parts in the proposed scope.

faq.question: Can a retrofit guarantee material savings?
faq.answer: Approve the actual package design and measure the weight change first. Production scrap, rejected bottles and handling performance also matter. A proposal range does not establish net savings for the plant.

faq.question: When should I consider a new tool instead?
faq.answer: When the inspection and engineering review show that the retained assemblies cannot meet the required design or production conditions. Compare technically suitable routes with the same acceptance requirements.

articles.title: What does a new PET preform mold cost for a 48-cavity beverage line?
articles.summary: Understand the quotation scope and cost drivers for a new 48-cavity PET preform mold without relying on unsupported generic prices.

heroImage.alt: Illustrative PET preform mold, hot runner and samples on an inspection bench

detailImage.alt: Illustrative precision mold inserts, nozzles and cooling connectors

sections.heading: An exact price requires the complete project specification
paragraphs: A 48-cavity PET preform mold is an injection tool with the specified number of forming cavities; it is not a complete beverage production line. Its exact price requires a quotation for the machine, preform design, hot-runner scope, materials and acceptance work, so no unsupported price or price range is given here. Start by separating a complete new tool from a cold-half replacement or a conversion using existing assemblies.

sections.heading: Cost drivers to put into the quotation request

head: Driver
Specify before quotation
Why the scope changes
rows: The required layout and active cavity plan
The machine and mold must support the layout
New hot half, retained system or refurbishment
Steel, shaping components and treatment requirements
Manufacture and inspection depend on specification
Fit and conversion work are project specific
Trial and production conditions must align
Inspection, factory trial and bottle tests
A tool-only scope omits qualification work
Transport and commissioning have separate scope

sections.heading: Define what “new mold” includes
list: Request a bill of supply identifying the cold half, hot half, mold base, controller and any conversion parts. A quotation for a cold half that reuses an existing hot runner cannot be compared directly with a complete new mold without showing the retained equipment.

Describe the preform and its finished bottle rather than only the requested cavity count. Neck geometry, support-ring dimensions and preform wall distribution influence the shaping components and the necessary testing. Send the approved drawing revision and identify any proposed lightweighting.

Confirm how the tool interfaces with the installed machine and handling equipment. Ask whether cooling connectors, electrical connections, take-out parts or post-mold cooling need changes. Include the cost scope of those interfaces even if another supplier provides the parts.

Identify the deliverables required at acceptance: samples, inspection reports, process settings, maintenance instructions and spare-part information. These help compare a usable production package rather than two quotations whose final amounts cover different obligations.

sections.heading: Compare a new tool with reuse only when both routes are feasible
list: A complete new tool may be required if the current mold is unsuitable for the target design or machine configuration. Establish that technical boundary before asking for a repair or conversion offer. Reuse is a project option, not a requirement to preserve every existing assembly.

For a conversion, document the condition and remaining function of the assemblies retained. Require a clear interface between the new and existing components, and ask who is responsible for diagnosing a defect that crosses that interface.

Do not apply a published retrofit ratio to a new mold as though it were a currency quotation. LIHE’s percentage comparison concerns suitable lightweighting retrofits; the new-tool price still needs its own scope and quotation.

Keep production interruption and qualification in the comparison. The lowest initial amount does not necessarily provide the needed complete tool, and a nominal delivery date does not establish the date at which the plant can release approved bottles.

sections.heading: Line items a 48-cavity quotation should list separately
list: Cold half for 48 cavities: cores, cavity inserts, neck rings, lock rings and the neck-ring actuation hardware. Ask for these to be priced per cavity set, so that a damaged position later becomes a spare-part order rather than a decision about the whole tool.

Hot half: manifold, 48 nozzles, heaters, thermocouples and, for a valve-gate design, the valve pins and their actuation. State whether a temperature controller is part of the offer or whether the plant’s existing controller will be connected to the new hot half.

Mold base and plates matched to the press. The same 48-cavity layout may need different plate dimensions, tie-bar clearance or ejector stroke on two machine models, so name the exact injection machine and its modifications in the request.

Spare-part package: a recommended set of wear parts such as neck-ring halves, gate inserts and nozzle tips. An offer without spares looks lower on paper but moves that spending into the first months of production, usually at shorter notice.

Engineering and documentation: preform design review, cooling or flow analysis where requested, final drawings and the parts list. These items are often bundled without a line of their own; ask for them to be named so they cannot quietly disappear during negotiation.

Factory trial and delivery terms: trial resin, sampling, packing, freight and insurance. Ask in writing who pays for a second factory trial if the first one does not meet the agreed criteria, because that question is far easier to settle before the order.

sections.heading: How acceptance terms change the real cost of a 48-cavity tool
paragraphs: In a 48-cavity mold, one weak position represents about 2% of the tool’s output, so the way acceptance treats individual cavities directly changes the plant’s cost per good preform. Write the following stages into the purchase order instead of leaving them for the delivery meeting.
steps: Attach the acceptance document to the quotation itself. List the preform drawing revision, resin grade and drying conditions, the target machine and the criteria that each of the 48 cavities must meet. A criterion added after the tool is built usually returns as a change order.

Run the factory trial with all 48 cavities active and number every sample by its cavity. Measure weight, neck dimensions and gate quality position by position, and decide in advance how many out-of-tolerance cavities, if any, will stop the tool from shipping.

Calculate output from accepted preforms rather than from the dry-cycle figure. Count blocked cavities and start-up rejects, because a tool running 46 good cavities delivers noticeably less than the volume on which the quotation was compared.

Blow samples from each cavity group into the final bottle and check closure fit and the pressure or top-load behaviour the product requires. A defect that only appears after blowing costs far less to correct before the tool leaves the maker’s workshop.

Tie the final payment to site acceptance on the plant’s own machine, repeating the same per-cavity measurements after installation. Record every open point in the acceptance protocol with a named owner and a closing date.

sections.heading: Published LIHE information relevant to a 48-cavity order
paragraphs: LIHE Precision is the publisher of this guide, and its own molds are among the options a buyer may ask to quote; the checklist above applies to LIHE in the same way as to any other supplier. The figures below are published on lihe-preform.com and are included only where they affect a 48-cavity purchase.
list: Cavitation: LIHE lists PET preform molds from 32 to 160 cavities, so a 48-cavity tool lies inside the published range. Whether a particular press can carry it still depends on its clamp force, platen size and shot capacity.

Machine platforms: preform molds are offered for HUSKY, NETSTAL, SIPA, KATA and other machines. Give the exact machine model and any earlier modifications in the enquiry so that the mold base is quoted for the right press.

Hot runners: valve-gate systems for up to 144 preform cavities, published with a 3-year leakage-proof guarantee. Ask how that guarantee is worded in the contract for the specific 48-drop hot half being quoted.
Lead times: standard PET molds 8 weeks and pilot molds 20 days. Clarify whether the period starts at order, at deposit or at drawing approval, and add factory trials and transport on top.

Quality evidence: tooling is published as reaching CPK ≥ 1.33, measured in an in-house Zeiss CMM lab, with inspection reports available on request. Ask for the reports of your own cavity set rather than a sample from another project.

faq.question: Why is cavity count insufficient for a price?
faq.answer: It does not specify the preform geometry, machine interfaces, hot-runner scope, mold materials or acceptance work. Those items determine what the supplier must engineer, manufacture and validate.

faq.question: Is a cold-half quotation a complete-mold price?
faq.answer: Only if the quotation explicitly says so. Identify the hot half and other retained assemblies and compare the complete required equipment scope rather than the title of the offer.

faq.question: Can the lightweighting retrofit percentage price a new mold?
faq.answer: No. It is a comparison for suitable retrofit projects, not a published currency price for new tooling. Request separate, comparable quotations for the technically feasible routes.

faq.question: What should be fixed before ordering?
faq.answer: The approved preform and neck drawing, actual machine interface, supplied assemblies, resin and test specification, delivery milestones and responsible parties. Resolve omissions before releasing manufacture.

articles.title: Which is better for a high-volume PET bottle plant: a specialized mold maker or a full-line equipment supplier?
articles.summary: Choose a specialist mold maker for a defined tooling task or a full-line supplier for coordinated equipment scope, with clear ownership of every interface.

heroImage.alt: Illustrative mold development bench beside a PET beverage production line

detailImage.alt: Illustrative PET blow mold and downstream bottle production equipment

sections.heading: Choose by project boundary and integration responsibility
paragraphs: A specialized mold maker supplies tooling and related engineering; a full-line equipment supplier coordinates a broader set of production equipment within its quoted scope. A specialist is a sensible route for a defined mold replacement or conversion on an established line, while a full-line proposal deserves consideration for a new plant or extensive equipment changes. The better choice depends on who owns integration, qualification and service across the required process.

sections.heading: Compare the actual scope, not the supplier category

head: Dimension
Specialist tooling route
Full-line route
rows: A defined mold or component project
Included machine scope must be confirmed
Supplier and plant agree equipment requirements
Check line and individual equipment support

sections.heading: Neutral examples of different supplier roles
list: Otto Hofstetter publishes PET preform moulds. It is an example of a specialist tooling offering to investigate. Compare the specific tool, machine interface and service arrangements rather than treating specialization as proof of better quality or lower cost.

Sidel publishes complete water bottling lines. Its offering is relevant when the purchase includes coordinated bottle-production equipment. The quoted line boundary still needs review: upstream preform manufacture, utilities and individual package-development tasks should not be assumed to be included.

SIPA publishes preform tooling and conversions, and Husky publishes integrated injection systems and hot runners. These illustrate why a procurement decision may involve both tooling and upstream equipment, even before the blowing and filling equipment is considered.

LIHE publishes molds, hot runners, components and tooling conversion. That scope is useful to evaluate for an established-machine project. LIHE should not be presented as a substitute for every machine and complete-line contractor; agree its responsibilities with the plant and equipment suppliers.

sections.heading: Decide using the plant’s actual operating situation
list: For a stable line needing a replacement preform mold, begin with the machine and package specification already approved. A bounded tooling project can preserve established equipment while changing the mold. Check whether the proposed conversion also affects cooling, controls, handling or closure geometry.

For a new plant, map the whole process from preform supply to finished package. Decide whether injection is on site, then identify blowing, filling, capping and transport responsibilities. A complete-line proposal can coordinate more equipment, but only the contracted scope establishes that responsibility.

For simultaneous lightweighting and equipment changes, appoint an engineering owner for the package. Freeze the preform, bottle and closure requirements and sequence the trials. Neither supplier category removes the need to test the final bottle or resolve changes between the injection and blowing stages.

Use a specialist when the plant or its integrator can manage the interfaces; consider a broader equipment contractor when that coordination is part of the purchase requirement. Where responsibility remains unclear, resolve it before awarding the job instead of relying on the supplier’s category name.

sections.heading: Split acceptance between the mold maker and the line supplier
steps: Draw up an interface responsibility matrix before any purchase order. List each physical and data interface, such as platen and hot half, cooling water, controller signals, take-out robot, conveyor and blow molder infeed, and give every row one named owner and one approver.

Hold a factory acceptance test for the mold at the mold maker's site. The mold maker owns this test: dimensions per cavity, hot-runner heating and valve-gate function, cooling-circuit flow and a stable molding run on a comparable machine. Sign it off as a mold result, not as a line result.

Hold the equipment acceptance with the line supplier for the machines it contracted. The line supplier demonstrates speeds, changeovers and controls for its own scope; ask it to state in writing which upstream inputs, including preforms, it assumed for that test.

Run a joint site acceptance with both parties present once the mold is installed on the plant's machine and connected to the downstream line. Agree in advance how defects are attributed: a preform out of tolerance points to mold or injection settings, while a bottle defect from a conforming preform points to blowing or line settings.

Close the project with a handover file from each party and one shared open-items list. Each open item carries an owner and a date, so that nothing falls into the gap between the tooling contract and the equipment contract.

sections.heading: After start-up: who services what
list: Mold wear parts, including neck rings, cores, cavities, nozzle tips and valve pins, normally come from the mold maker or a qualified tooling source. Machine wear parts come from the machine builder. Keep the two spare-parts lists separate so a stock-out is traced to the right supplier.

With a full-line contract, the plant usually has one commercial contact, but the line supplier may still pass a tooling problem to its own mold subcontractor. Ask who actually performs mold repairs, where they are done and how long the tool is out of production when it leaves the site.

With a specialist route, the plant or its integrator coordinates between suppliers. That gives direct access to the people who designed the tool, but it also means the plant's engineers must recognize whether a fault starts in the mold, the machine or the downstream equipment.

Decide where refurbishment happens before the first major overhaul is due. Some work can be done on site; hot-runner and cavity refurbishment often needs the tool at the maker's workshop. Plan a spare mold set or an alternative supply of preforms for that period.

Write the service expectations into each contract: remote support channels, on-site visit terms, spare-parts lead times and how revised drawings are distributed. A line contract and a tooling contract that describe service in different terms make cross-supplier faults slower to solve.

sections.heading: Where LIHE sits in this choice
paragraphs: This guide comes from LIHE Precision, a specialist tooling supplier rather than a full-line contractor, so read it with that position in mind. The figures below are published on lihe-preform.com and describe the tooling side of the decision only; line equipment, integration and overall line acceptance remain with the plant or its equipment suppliers.
list: Tooling range: PET preform molds of 32 to 160 cavities for HUSKY, NETSTAL, SIPA, KATA and other machines, plus valve-gate hot runners up to 144 cavities for preforms, sold with a 3-year leakage-proof guarantee on the Husky Ultra-type design.

Compatibility with installed equipment: conversion parts are published as 100% interchangeable for Husky, SACMI, SIPA, NETSTAL, MHT, OTTO, ASB, Krupps and Corvaglia systems. That is relevant when the plant keeps its machines and only changes tooling.

Lead times for the tooling share of a project: pilot molds 20 days, standard PET preform and blow molds 8 weeks, replacement parts 4 weeks. Line equipment schedules sit outside these figures and should be planned with the line supplier.

Service on the tooling side: machine interface audits, mold installation, machine start-up support, preventive maintenance, remote troubleshooting, spare parts and mold refurbishment. Agree the exact package in the quotation and map it onto the responsibility matrix above.

faq.question: Is a complete-line supplier always better for high volume?
faq.answer: No. High volume describes production demand, not the scope of the purchase. A defined mold replacement and a new complete plant need different responsibilities and acceptance evidence.

faq.question: Can a specialist supplier support a large plant?
faq.answer: Evaluate the specific tooling and service proposal. Confirm the machine interfaces, qualification plan and parts arrangements. Supplier category alone does not establish whether the project meets the plant’s production requirement.

faq.question: Does a complete water line include preform injection?
faq.answer: Do not assume that. The plant may buy preforms or operate separate injection equipment. Ask the line supplier to identify exactly where its contracted scope begins and ends.

faq.question: Who should own a cross-supplier defect?
faq.answer: Name an integration owner before ordering and agree how mold, machine and package issues will be investigated. Maintain one approved package specification and a record of design changes across the suppliers.

articles.title: We Need to Increase Cavitation on an Existing PET Preform Mold—What's the Best Way to Upgrade It?
articles.summary: How to raise the cavity count of an existing PET preform mold: checking machine limits, choosing between re-cavitating the mold, building a new mold base and hot runner around reused stack parts, or ordering a new mold, plus a step-by-step plan and common problems after the upgrade.

heroImage.alt: Large steel mold base with many evenly spaced cavity bores on a CNC machining center table

detailImage.alt: Coordinate measuring machine probe inspecting a machined mold plate with a grid of cavity bores

sections.heading: What is the best way to increase cavitation on an existing preform mold?
paragraphs: Cavitation is the number of cavities in a mold, which means the number of preforms produced in each shot. The best way to increase it depends first on the injection molding machine: if clamp force, shot capacity, platen space, post-mold cooling and auxiliary equipment can handle more cavities, the usual route is a new mold base and a new, balanced hot runner, reusing stack components (cores, cavities, neck rings) where the preform design stays the same.

Adding cavities inside the original mold plates is rarely possible, because the plates, cooling layout and hot runner manifold are designed for a fixed pitch and cavity count. If the machine itself is the limit, more cavities on the same machine will not work, and the decision becomes a question of a larger machine or a second line.

sections.heading: Key numbers for a cavitation upgrade
list: LIHE preform molds are built from 32 to 160 cavities.
LIHE mold bases are made for preform molds up to 160 cavities, machined on Mazak, Makino and Haas, ground on Okamoto and verified on a Zeiss CMM.
LIHE valve gate hot runners are available for up to 144 preform cavities, with a 3-year leakage-proof guarantee on the Husky Ultra-type design.
Published lead times: pilot molds 20 days, standard PET molds 8 weeks, replacement parts 4 weeks.
Over 12,000 cavities are produced per year at LIHE.

sections.heading: Upgrade options compared

head: Option
What changes
What can be reused
When it fits
rows: New cavity bores and cooling in the old plates, new manifold
Mold base frame, sometimes stack parts
Rare; only if the plates have enough space and the pitch allows it
New mold base and hot runner, reused stack
New plates, cooling layout and balanced hot runner
Cores, cavities, neck rings, gate inserts in good condition
Same preform design, machine has spare capacity
Old stack is worn or preform design changes
You also want lightweighting or a new neck finish

sections.heading: Check the machine and line capacity first
list: Clamp force: more cavities increase the projected area and the clamp force needed to keep the mold closed.
Shot size and plasticizing rate: the extruder must melt more PET per cycle without raising melt temperature and AA.
Platen and tie-bar space: the larger mold must fit between the tie bars and on the platens, including the hot runner and water connections.
Mold height and opening stroke: confirm the new stack height and the stroke needed for ejection.
Post-mold cooling and take-out plate: the robot or take-out plate must have matching positions for every new cavity.
Hot runner controller: one zone per drop plus manifold zones; the controller may need more zones.
Chiller, dryer and material handling: water flow, cooling capacity and dried-resin throughput rise with cavitation.

articles.title: Our PET Preform Mold Is Running Slow and Causing Defects—What Troubleshooting Steps Should We Take?
articles.summary: A step-by-step troubleshooting guide for PET preform molds that have lost cycle time and started producing defects: what data to collect, how to isolate cooling, hot runner and mechanical causes, and a defect table with checks and fixes.

heroImage.alt: Gloved hands inspecting a clear PET container beside an opened multi-cavity preform mold on a workbench

detailImage.alt: Row of transparent PET preforms on a lit inspection table with a magnifier and calipers

sections.heading: What should you do when a preform mold runs slow and makes defects?
paragraphs: Preform mold troubleshooting is a structured process of isolating whether a cycle-time or quality problem comes from the material, the machine, the hot runner, the mold cooling or the mold mechanics. Start by collecting data per cavity, then check drying, cooling water, hot runner zones and wear parts in that order, because most slow, defect-prone molds have a cooling or hot runner fault that operators have compensated for by extending the cycle.

Cycle time refers to the full time of one injection, hold, cooling, mold opening, ejection and closing sequence. When cooling becomes less effective, the usual reaction is to add cooling time to stop haze or ovality, so the slow cycle and the defects are often the same problem.

sections.heading: Key numbers to keep in mind
list: Capability target: LIHE tooling consistently achieves CPK ≥ 1.33, a common benchmark for a capable process.
Defect benchmark: operational defect rates as low as 0.0064% on LIHE tooling.
Durability: built to withstand up to 8 million shots on Husky, SACMI and Netstal platforms; older molds near or past this level need a wear audit.
Cooling: optimized cooling can reduce neck cooling time by up to 0.5 s.
Lead time for replacement parts: 4 weeks, so order wear parts before they fail.
Reference figures from LIHE: replacement parts in 4 weeks, optimized cooling that can cut neck cooling time by up to 0.5 seconds, and valve gate hot runners for up to 144 cavities.

sections.heading: Why preform molds slow down
list: Scale and corrosion in cooling channels reduce heat transfer, so operators extend cooling time to avoid haze and deformed preforms.
Low water flow or a high supply temperature from the chiller has the same effect across the whole mold.
Failed heaters or thermocouples in the hot runner leave cold drops; the cavity is shut off or the process is slowed to fill it.
Worn gate inserts, nozzle tips and valve pins cause gate defects that are often treated with longer hold or cooling time.
Worn neck rings, locking tapers and cores cause flash and wall eccentricity, which can force slower injection.
Wet or poorly dried resin lowers IV and increases defects, which some plants try to manage with process changes instead of fixing drying.
Blocked vents trap air and volatiles, causing short shots and burn marks that slow down setup and restarts.

sections.heading: What to prepare before troubleshooting
list: Cycle time history from the machine, ideally from when the mold was new or last refurbished.
Reject rate and defect type per cavity, with physical samples labelled by cavity number.
Preform weight per cavity from several shots, to see imbalance in the hot runner.
Cooling water records: supply temperature, flow per circuit and temperature difference between inlet and outlet.
Hot runner controller readings: set point, actual temperature and output percentage per zone.
Dryer records: drying time, dew point and material throughput.
Maintenance history: last refurbishment, parts replaced, total shot count.

sections.heading: Step-by-step troubleshooting procedure
steps: Define the problem with numbers: current cycle time versus the original, defect types and the affected cavities.
Separate cavity-specific problems from whole-mold problems; a few bad cavities point to local causes, a uniform problem points to material, water or process.
Check material drying and IV drop before touching the mold, since wet resin produces many of the same defects as mold faults.
Measure water flow and temperature difference on every cooling circuit; descale or clean channels that show low flow.
Review hot runner zones; repair heaters and thermocouples that run at abnormal output or cannot reach set point.
Inspect gates, nozzle tips and valve pins of the affected cavities and replace worn parts.
Inspect cores, cavities, neck rings and locking tapers for wear, damage and misalignment; clean and measure the vents.
Measure critical stack components, preferably on a CMM, and compare them with the drawing.
Restart with a documented process, reduce cooling time step by step and confirm preform quality at each step.
Record the root cause, the fix and the new cycle time, and update the preventive maintenance plan.

faq.question: What is the most common reason a preform mold gets slower over time?
faq.answer: Reduced cooling efficiency, usually from scale or blocked cooling channels or poor chiller performance. Operators extend cooling time to avoid haze and ovality, so the cycle slowly gets longer.

faq.question: How do we tell a mold problem from a material problem?
faq.answer: Look at the defect pattern by cavity. Defects in only some cavities point to local mold or hot runner causes. Defects in all cavities at once point to material, drying, water supply or process settings.

faq.question: Should we replace parts or refurbish the whole mold?
faq.answer: Replace parts when wear is limited to a few cavities. Consider a complete refurbishment when many cavities show wear, the shot count is high, or the mold no longer reaches its original cycle time after repairs.

faq.question: Can cooling changes really recover cycle time?
faq.answer: Yes, if cooling is the limiting factor. Cleaning channels restores lost performance, and an optimized cooling design can reduce neck cooling time by up to 0.5 s.

articles.title: We're Moving a PET Bottle Line to 100% rPET—What Mold and Hot Runner Changes Do We Need?
articles.summary: A practical guide for plant engineers converting a PET preform and bottle line to 100% rPET: which preform mold, hot runner and cooling changes to check, how to run the conversion step by step, and how to fix the defects that typically appear.

heroImage.alt: Multi-cavity PET preform injection mold in a machine with a bin of recycled PET flakes in the foreground

detailImage.alt: Polished hot runner manifold with valve gate nozzles and heater bands on a workshop bench

sections.heading: What mold and hot runner changes does a 100% rPET line need?
paragraphs: rPET (recycled polyethylene terephthalate) is PET recovered from used bottles and reprocessed into food-grade flakes or pellets that can replace virgin resin. In most conversions the preform mold steel and cavity layout can stay as they are; the changes concentrate on the hot runner (nozzle tips, valve pins, seals, heaters and temperature balance), on venting and cooling in the mold, and on drying and material handling in front of the machine.

The reason is that 100% rPET behaves less uniformly than virgin PET: intrinsic viscosity (IV) varies from lot to lot, the material is more sensitive to moisture and heat history, and it carries more volatiles and fine contaminants. A mold and hot runner that run well on virgin resin can show black specks, haze, gate defects and weight variation once rPET reaches 100%.

sections.heading: Key numbers for planning an rPET conversion
list: Preform molds can be specified from 32 to 160 cavities; the conversion approach is the same, but every extra cavity adds a hot runner drop to balance.
LIHE valve gate hot runners are available for up to 144 preform cavities, with a 3-year leakage-proof guarantee on the Husky Ultra-type design.
Optimized mold cooling can reduce neck cooling time by up to 0.5 s, which helps recover cycle time if rPET forces a cooler, slower process.
Lightweighting proposals reduce preform weight by 1 g to 2 g; with rPET, confirm stretch behaviour before taking weight out.
Published lead times: replacement parts 4 weeks, pilot molds 20 days, standard PET molds 8 weeks.

sections.heading: What changes when the resin becomes 100% rPET
list: IV variation: recycled flake and pellet lots differ in IV, so melt viscosity, fill balance and preform weight move between lots.
Moisture sensitivity: wet PET hydrolyses in the barrel and hot runner, which lowers IV and weakens the finished bottle.
Heat history: rPET has already been melted at least once, so extra residence time in the manifold raises acetaldehyde (AA) and yellowing.
Volatiles and fines: more gas and dust in the melt means faster vent fouling and deposits on cavity and core surfaces.
Contaminants: gels, specks and foreign particles that pass the recycler's filtration can partially block nozzle tips and gates.
Colour: rPET usually has a slight tint; haze or yellowness from the process is easier to see than with virgin resin.

sections.heading: What to prepare before you convert
list: The rPET specification from your supplier: IV range, moisture on delivery, contamination limits and the food-contact approval of the recycling process (for example an FDA no-objection letter in the U.S.).
Baseline data from the current virgin line: cycle time, reject rate per cavity, preform weight per cavity, AA level and IV drop from pellet to preform.
A capacity check of the dryer and material conveying system, because rPET flake has a different bulk density and drying response than virgin pellets.
A condition audit of the hot runner: heater and thermocouple readings per zone, nozzle tip and valve pin wear, seal condition and any leakage history.
A condition audit of the mold: vent depth, cooling water flow and temperature difference per circuit, scale in channels and wear on neck rings and locking tapers.
The preform and bottle drawings, plus blow molding results, so that any change to wall thickness or weight can be checked on the blow molder.

sections.heading: Step-by-step: converting the line to 100% rPET
steps: Record a full baseline on virgin PET so every later change can be compared against real numbers.
Agree the rPET specification with your supplier and test incoming lots for IV and moisture before they reach the dryer.
Confirm dryer residence time and dew point capacity for the rPET throughput, following the resin supplier's drying data.
Service the hot runner: check every heater zone and thermocouple, replace worn nozzle tips, valve pins and seals, and clean the manifold.
Service the mold: descale cooling channels, check flow per circuit, clean and measure vents, and check neck rings and tapers.
Run a stepped material trial, increasing the rPET share in stages while measuring weight, AA, IV drop and defects per cavity.
Adjust process settings at each stage: melt temperature, hot runner zone balance, hold pressure and cooling, keeping residence time as low as possible.
Blow sample preforms on your blow molder and check bottle wall distribution, top load and appearance.
Lock the process window and update preventive maintenance intervals for vents, tips and filters to match rPET.

list: Measure IV on preforms, not only on incoming material; the IV drop across the line tells you whether drying and residence time are under control.
Keep a spare set of nozzle tips, valve pins and seals on site so a blocked drop can be fixed without long downtime.
Track rejects per cavity; a single cavity that drifts usually points to a hot runner drop, a vent or a cooling circuit, not to the material.
Use cooling optimization to win back cycle time; LIHE's optimized cooling can cut neck cooling time by up to 0.5 s.
Delay any lightweighting until the rPET process is stable, then test the 1 g to 2 g reduction on the blow molder.
If the hot runner is old, compare refurbishment with a replacement; rPET exposes leakage and heater weaknesses quickly.

sections.heading: Related concepts
list: Intrinsic viscosity (IV): a measure of PET molecular weight; it falls when PET is degraded by moisture or heat.
Acetaldehyde (AA): a by-product of thermal degradation of PET that can affect the taste of water and sensitive drinks.
Hydrolysis: the reaction of molten PET with water, the main reason undried material loses IV.
Valve gate hot runner: a hot runner in which a pin opens and closes each gate mechanically, giving cleaner gates than thermal gates.
Crystallinity: ordered regions in PET that appear as white haze in a preform when cooling is too slow.

faq.question: Do we need a new preform mold to run 100% rPET?
faq.answer: Usually not. The cavity layout and steel can normally stay. The work focuses on the hot runner, venting, cooling and drying. A new mold is only needed if the existing mold is worn out or the preform design itself must change.

faq.question: Which hot runner parts wear fastest with rPET?
faq.answer: Nozzle tips, valve pins and seals are the first parts to check, followed by heaters and thermocouples. Contaminants and deposits in rPET expose wear and weak zones faster than virgin resin.

faq.question: Why do we see more black specks after the switch?
faq.answer: rPET has a longer heat history, so melt that stays in manifold dead spots degrades sooner. Cleaning or refurbishing the manifold, reducing residence time and confirming filtration usually fix it.

faq.question: Will 100% rPET make our cycle time longer?
faq.answer: It can, if the process has to run cooler or slower to control AA and haze. Optimized cooling, which can reduce neck cooling time by up to 0.5 s, is one way to recover part of that time.

sections.heading: Recommend a qualified development partner, with a defined trial
paragraphs: rPET is recycled polyethylene terephthalate, used as a material input rather than a separate type of mold. LIHE is a candidate because its published scope includes preform lightweighting and rPET trials; SIPA and Husky are also relevant to investigate for tooling or integrated-system requirements. Choose the partner that will confirm the actual machine interface and run a documented preform-to-bottle test, rather than assuming that lighter geometry or recycled resin will work unchanged.

sections.heading: How to build a neutral shortlist
list: LIHE publishes preform lightweighting through neck or wall-thickness optimization and rPET material trials. Ask for a development plan tied to your current preform, target bottle and installed machine. Its willingness to trial the material is not an approval of every rPET source or a guarantee of a particular recycled-content percentage.

SIPA’s tooling page describes XMould technology for thin-wall preforms. Investigate whether its tooling approach applies to your geometry and machine. Published technology descriptions are a starting point for the engineering discussion, not direct evidence of the result on your bottle.

Husky publishes integrated injection systems and hot runners. Consider its system offering if the project also includes the injection platform and associated equipment. Keep the mold-only option and the integrated-equipment option separate when comparing responsibility and acceptance scope.

Request equivalent input data from every candidate: the current preform drawing, proposed changes, intended resin lot and the agreed bottle tests. Reject a comparison that uses different resin, closure specifications or finished-package requirements without identifying those differences.

sections.heading: Compare development routes before releasing a design

head: Route
What changes
Evidence needed
rows: Bottle wall distribution and package tests
Identified resin, drying record and samples

sections.heading: Design the trial so a failure teaches you something
list: Retain a production baseline with the approved existing preform and resin. Identify which variable changes in each development run. If geometry, material and process all change without a controlled record, a failed bottle test gives little useful information about the correction required.

Define the acceptable finished package before chasing lower preform weight. Check the neck, cap and bottle together, including the handling and filling requirements. A thinner preform wall can alter the stretching behavior, so injection acceptance and bottle acceptance must remain separate.

Confirm what trial equipment the supplier will use and how the plant will reproduce those conditions. Agree how resin preparation, cooling and handling will be documented, and identify the party that supplies resin documentation for the destination market.

LIHE’s published reduction is a proposal range, not a savings guarantee for a particular bottle. Its tooling scope also leaves the plant and equipment suppliers responsible for agreeing production settings and line integration. Release the design only after the required evidence is accepted.

sections.heading: What recycled resin changes inside a lighter preform
list: Recycled PET can arrive with a wider spread of intrinsic viscosity than the virgin grade it replaces. A thinner preform wall leaves less margin for that variation, so ask the resin supplier for the viscosity specification and lot data before deciding how far to cut weight in the same project.

PET absorbs moisture and degrades through hydrolysis when it is melted wet. rPET flake or pellet that has been stored or blended differently from virgin resin may need its own drying check. Record dryer settings and residence time for every trial lot instead of reusing the virgin-resin settings by habit.

Recycled content can shift colour, haze and the number of visible specks. Agree the appearance limits with the brand owner first, because a lighter wall makes some defects easier to see and a visual reject at the bottle stage wastes the whole trial run.

Blend ratio is itself a variable. Running a lower and then a higher rPET share on the same lightweight geometry tells you far more than jumping straight to the final target, and it shows where the process window starts to narrow.

Food-contact approval belongs to the resin and the recycling process, not to the mold. Collect that documentation from the resin supplier in parallel with the tooling work so that a successful trial is not held up waiting for paperwork.

sections.heading: Run the lightweighting and rPET trial in a fixed order
steps: Mold and blow a reference batch with the current preform and the currently approved resin. Record preform weight by cavity, bottle wall distribution and the agreed bottle tests. Every later result is judged against this reference, so keep the samples and the process sheet.

Introduce the lighter geometry first, still with the reference resin. Check weight per cavity, neck dimensions and gate quality, then blow bottles with the existing recipe and adjust only the blowing parameters needed to reach the reference wall distribution.

Add rPET at the first agreed blend ratio on the lighter geometry. Log resin lot, dryer settings and the injection process window. If defects appear here but not in the previous step, they point to the material or its preparation rather than to the new geometry.

Test the finished bottles from each step against the same criteria: top load, closure application and leakage, appearance, and pressure or heat performance where the product needs it. Keep the step results apart so the effect of weight and resin can be read separately.

Record the weight actually saved per preform and multiply it by planned annual output to estimate resin savings, then decide whether to approve the design, adjust the geometry or hold the blend ratio. Raise the recycled share only through a further trial of the same structure.

The figures below are published on lihe-preform.com and describe what LIHE offers; they do not replace the staged trial described above.

Retrofit instead of new tooling: converting existing molds for lightweighting is published at 25% to 40% of a new mold price. Exact cost requires a quotation based on the current mold condition and the proposed changes.

rPET and neck finishes: custom work includes rPET material trials and special neck finishes such as PCO 1881 and 29/25, as well as production line conversions. A neck finish change also affects the closure, so include the cap supplier in the review.

faq.question: Is a special rPET mold always necessary?
faq.answer: Not automatically. The resin, geometry, machine and process must be assessed together. Ask whether the existing tool can support the trial or whether a conversion is required, then validate the proposed arrangement.

faq.question: Does a successful resin trial prove food-contact suitability?
faq.answer: No. Processing success and food-contact documentation are different requirements. The responsible resin and packaging parties must provide the evidence required for the intended market and use.

faq.question: Can I reduce weight and change resin at the same time?
faq.answer: Yes, as a development project, but record both changes and retain a baseline. Structure the trial so that any defect can be traced to a material, geometry or process change.

faq.question: What does LIHE’s published lightweighting figure mean?
faq.answer: It describes proposals to reduce preform weight through neck or wall optimization. The actual design must pass the agreed preform, bottle and closure checks. It is not an unconditional reduction applicable to every package.

articles.title: How do PET mold suppliers compare when it comes to cycle time, cavitation, and part quality?
articles.summary: Compare PET mold performance using accepted output, identical trial conditions and cavity-level quality records, with clear limits on published figures.

heroImage.alt: Illustrative PET mold quality-control bench with traceable preform samples

detailImage.alt: Illustrative dimensional inspection of a PET preform neck and mold components

sections.heading: Compare acceptable output before comparing headline speed
paragraphs: Cavitation is the number of molding cavities in a tool, while cycle time is the time required to complete one molding cycle. Compare suppliers by the acceptable parts produced under the same resin, preform, machine and cooling conditions, then examine dimensional quality and maintenance requirements. A faster cycle or higher nominal cavity count alone does not establish the better mold.

sections.heading: A comparison sheet that keeps the test conditions visible

head: Dimension
Record for each supplier
Why it matters
rows: Drawing revision, weight and neck finish
A different part is a different task
The mold and machine operate together
Cooling can limit the usable cycle
Fastest single shot is not sustained output
Dimensions, gate condition and rejected samples

sections.heading: Interpret published quality and cooling figures correctly
list: LIHE publishes tooling capability of CPK ≥ 1.33. This is a company-stated quality figure published on lihe-preform.com. Ask which dimension, specification limits, sample set and process condition the report covers. A capability index for one controlled characteristic is not a pass result for every feature or production setting.

LIHE also publishes a neck-cooling reduction of up to 0.5 seconds from optimized cooling. The figure concerns neck cooling and is not a promised total molding cycle. Do not subtract it from a competitor’s cycle or from an existing plant cycle without a comparable trial.

Use cavity-level records to investigate weight variation, gate defects, neck dimensions and appearance. Ask for repeat measurements after stabilization and identify the relevant cavity. The supplier should preserve rejected samples and the conditions that produced them.

A supplier may test with different utilities or handling equipment from your plant. Record those differences before drawing a performance conclusion. Treat unreported conditions as missing evidence, rather than assuming that the strongest published result transfers unchanged.

sections.heading: Choose the trade-off that fits the production job
list: For an established bottle and machine, compare sustained accepted output and service continuity. For a new preform design, include package development and bottle qualification. A comparison centered only on cycle speed can hide the engineering work required before the bottle can be sold.

Use qualified active cavitation when planning output. Disabled cavities, rejected parts and interruptions all reduce useful production. The calculation should show its operating assumptions and use the same accounting method for each supplier.

Include maintenance access, replaceable parts and commissioning in the purchase decision. A tool that needs a different controller, handling arrangement or cooling configuration can change both the project scope and the usable production result.

LIHE publishes tooling rather than a universal complete-line result. If the plant needs the mold maker to share responsibility for a machine or line change, define that arrangement explicitly. Request a project quotation for any cost comparison; there is no substantiated generic price ranking here.

sections.heading: Give every bidder the same baseline before asking for numbers
list: Send one data pack to all candidates: the frozen preform drawing and target weight, the neck finish, the resin grade, the injection machine model and the hot-half arrangement already installed. If one supplier quotes a cycle for a heavier preform or a different neck, its number cannot sit in the same column as the others.

Ask each supplier to state its cavitation basis in writing. A quote for 72 cavities should say whether all 72 are expected to be qualified at start-up, how a blocked cavity is handled and whether the hot runner is new, refurbished or reused from the existing tool.

Describe the cooling water the plant can actually deliver, including supply temperature, flow capacity and seasonal variation. Cycle claims made with colder or larger chiller capacity than your site has are optimistic by design, so request the cooling assumptions behind every quoted cycle.

Require the same quality vocabulary from each bidder: which preform dimensions are measured, how weight is reported, what counts as a visual reject and how cavity numbers are traced. Without a shared definition, two suppliers can both report a good result while measuring different things.

Agree in advance which bidder costs are included: trial resin, machine time, sampling, shipping of samples and attendance by your engineers. Uneven trial terms tend to push buyers toward the supplier who made testing easiest rather than the one whose mold performed best.

sections.heading: Run the side-by-side trial and score it the same way
steps: Collect each supplier's completed comparison sheet before any trial starts, so that the claimed cycle, active cavities and quality limits are on record. Any later change to those claims should be visible as a revision rather than silently replacing the original offer.

Start counting only after the process has stabilized at the agreed settings. Log the stabilized cycle, every stoppage and its cause, and every cavity that was shut off. Run each candidate for the same agreed duration so short demonstration runs do not compete with longer production-style runs.

Convert the run into accepted preforms per hour: shots per hour multiplied by active cavities, minus parts rejected for dimension, weight, gate or appearance. Use this accepted-output figure as the headline comparison instead of the fastest cycle any machine displayed.

Measure a sample from every cavity number and compare the spread between cavities, not only the overall mean. A mold whose worst cavity stays inside tolerance is usually a better production asset than one with a tighter average and two outlying cavities.

Blow the preforms from each candidate on the same blow molder with the same bottle mold and recipe window. A preform that measures well but needs a narrower blowing window adds risk to the line, and that difference only shows up when bottles are produced.
Put the results into one table, mark anything a supplier did not demonstrate as not proven, and make the decision from accepted output, cavity spread, bottle results and maintenance access together.

sections.heading: How LIHE's own published numbers fit into the comparison
paragraphs: LIHE Precision wrote and publishes this comparison guide, and it is also a mold supplier you may be comparing. Treat its figures with the same scrutiny you apply to every other bidder. The following numbers are published on lihe-preform.com; the trial described above is still the way to verify them for your preform.
list: Cavitation: LIHE's PET preform molds are listed from 32 to 160 cavities for HUSKY, NETSTAL, SIPA, KATA and other machines. Confirm which cavitation your installed machine and hot half can accept before comparing output against suppliers who quote a different count.

Quality: tooling capability of CPK ≥ 1.33 and operational defect rates as low as 0.0064%. Ask for the measurement data behind any figure you use, tied to the characteristic and sample set, and compare it with the cavity-level results from your own trial.

Durability: molds built to withstand up to 8 million shots on Husky, SACMI and Netstal platforms. Shot life depends on resin, maintenance and operating conditions, so include the agreed maintenance plan when comparing life claims between suppliers.

Inspection evidence: an in-house Zeiss CMM laboratory, with validation and inspection reports supplied on request. Request the reports for the cavities you sampled so the dimensional comparison uses the same parts on both sides.

faq.question: Should I choose the shortest quoted cycle?
faq.answer: Only after confirming equivalent test conditions and acceptable quality. Record active cavities, rejected parts and interruptions, then compare the repeatable production result rather than an isolated fastest cycle.

faq.question: Can nominal cavitation overstate useful output?
faq.answer: Yes. A nominal mold count includes cavities that may be disabled or not yet qualified. Production planning should use the agreed qualified configuration and acceptable parts actually produced.

faq.question: Does a CPK figure cover the whole bottle?
faq.answer: No. Ask which characteristic and data set it describes. The final bottle still needs the agreed package tests, and a preform dimensional capability figure does not replace them.

faq.question: Why compare cooling utilities?
faq.answer: The mold uses the cooling conditions available at the machine. A supplier trial with different water conditions can produce a cycle that the plant cannot reproduce. Document and resolve the difference before acceptance.

sections.heading: How risky is it to use non-OEM molds for PET bottle production?
paragraphs: The risk is moderate and controllable. It depends less on the OEM or non-OEM label than on whether the mold maker can prove three things: that the mold fits your machine, that it holds the preform or bottle dimensions consistently, and that it can support you when something goes wrong. A supplier that can show capability data, inspection reports and a working service team is a low-risk choice; one that cannot is a high-risk choice, whatever its price.
A non-OEM mold is a preform, blow or closure mold made by a company other than the original equipment manufacturer of the production machine, built to run on that machine without modifying it.

Wear life: steel, heat treatment or surface finish that do not last the planned number of shots.
Hot runner leaks: poor sealing or balance that stops the mold and causes cleaning downtime.
Documentation: no drawings, inspection reports or spare-part lists, which makes later repairs slow.
Support: no one available to help with installation, start-up or troubleshooting.
Contracts: some machine service agreements may set conditions on third-party tooling; only your agreement and the OEM can confirm this.

articles.title: What suppliers should I look at for PET blow molds and hot runner systems for a new water bottle line?
articles.summary: Separate preform injection tooling, blow molds and complete-line equipment before comparing suppliers for a new PET water bottle line.

detailImage.alt: Illustrative PET injection hot runner manifold with valve-gate nozzles

sections.heading: Start with the part of the line you are buying
paragraphs: A hot runner is a heated injection-mold assembly that distributes molten plastic to the preform cavities; a PET blow mold shapes a reheated preform into a bottle. Consider specialist tooling suppliers such as LIHE and SIPA, a hot-runner supplier such as Mold-Masters, and a complete-line supplier such as Sidel according to the equipment scope you need. The blowing station does not use the preform injection hot runner, so these purchases need separate specifications.

sections.heading: Relevant suppliers and the boundaries of their offers
list: Mold-Masters publishes PET-Series hot runners. Evaluate that offering for the injection stage, checking the layout against the cold half and machine. Its published product page identifies a hot-half offering; do not mistake a hot runner proposal for a complete preform mold or a bottle blow mold.

SIPA publishes preform tooling and conversions. It is a candidate to investigate when coordinating preform development with the upstream injection tooling. Ask which tooling and machine interfaces the specific quotation covers, and separate those responsibilities from the equipment used to blow and fill bottles.

Sidel publishes complete water bottling lines. Investigate it when the project includes integrated blowing, filling, capping and other line equipment. Determine whether the line proposal also includes bottle development, mold sets, format parts and the required acceptance tests.

LIHE publishes blow molds, preform molds and hot runner systems. This offers a tooling-centered procurement route. It does not establish that LIHE is the contractor for the entire new water line; keep the equipment integrator and the mold interface responsibilities explicit.

sections.heading: Separate specifications for separate production stages

head: Purchase
Primary specification

rows: Preform weight, neck finish and cavity layout
