Bottle geometry, base and filling method
Blower mold carrier and neck handling

sections.heading: Water-bottle design decisions that affect the tooling order
list: Decide whether the plant will buy finished preforms or manufacture them. If preforms are purchased, a new blowing and filling line may not require a new injection mold or hot runner at all. Keep supplier selection aligned with the actual production route.

Approve the water-bottle geometry and neck finish before ordering the complete mold set. The bottle base, label area and handling geometry affect equipment beyond the blower. Ask the integrator to confirm the full format-parts list alongside the approved bottle drawing.

Specify the filling method and product requirements instead of selecting tooling from the beverage name alone. Still water, sparkling water and other beverages can have different package requirements. Cold-fill, hot-fill and aseptic processes should be identified explicitly in the design brief.

Request consistent drawings across the preform, bottle and closure. A change to the preform neck may require changes to handling parts and capping, while a bottle-body change may primarily affect blow tooling and downstream transport. Resolve these boundaries before comparing commercial offers.

sections.heading: Draw the interface lines between the three supply scopes
list: Injection side: the hot runner supplier and the preform mold supplier share the hot-half to cold-half interface, including nozzle positions, gate geometry, heater zones, connectors and cooling connections. If two companies are involved, name one of them as responsible for the assembled mold, or record in writing that the plant is the integrator.

Injection to blowing: the preform drawing is the contract between the mold maker and the blower. The neck finish and support ring must suit the blower’s neck handling, and the preform body must suit its heating oven. Both sides should sign the same preform revision before any steel is cut.

Blowing side: the blow mold supplier needs the blower model, the mold carrier type and the approved bottle drawing. A water bottle for a two-step blower is specified differently from one for a one-step machine, where injection and blowing take place on the same platform.

Blowing to filling and capping: the bottle neck, body and base interact with conveyors, star wheels, neck grippers, the filler and the capper. These format parts often belong to the line supplier’s scope, so confirm who designs them for each bottle size.

Utilities: the plant should state the cooling water available for the injection mold and the blow molds and the compressed-air supply for blowing, so that each supplier designs for the same conditions and no trial relies on utilities the site does not have.

sections.heading: Accept the water line stage by stage, not only at the end
steps: Approve the bottle, preform and closure drawings together, with the line integrator, the mold maker and the hot runner supplier signing the same revisions. Every later change then has a clear owner and a clear cost.

Test the hot runner on its own before it is matched to the cold half: heating of every zone, temperature stability and freedom from leakage. Record the results against the serial number of the hot half.

Run the assembled preform mold and check each cavity for weight, neck dimensions and gate quality. If the plant will buy preforms instead of making them, apply this step to samples from the preform supplier.

Blow the trial preforms on the target blower, or an equivalent machine, with the actual blow molds. Check wall distribution, base shape and filled volume for each bottle size, for example 500 ml and 1.5 L.

Run filled and capped bottles through the line and record leaks, closure application results and handling faults. List each open item against the supplier responsible for the interface where it appeared.

paragraphs: This guide comes from LIHE Precision, a company that supplies molds and hot runners but does not build complete filling lines; weigh its advice with that position in mind. The figures below are published on lihe-preform.com and cover only the tooling scopes discussed in this article.
list: Blow molds for two-step blowers from SIDEL, KRONES, SIG/KHS, TECH-LONG and NEWAMSTAR and for one-step machines from SIPA, ASB and AOKI, including KHS InnoPET Blomax and Krones Contiform cold-fill sets and split-type quick-change molds.
Published water-bottle sizes: 330 ml, 500 ml, 550 ml and 1.5 L. Any other size has to be confirmed in the quotation.
Hot runners: valve-gate designs for up to 144 preform cavities, compatible with HUSKY, NETSTAL, KM and SIPA machines. The Husky Ultra-type design carries a 3-year leakage-proof guarantee.
If the plant will make its own preforms, the injection tooling covers PET preform molds of 32 to 160 cavities for HUSKY, NETSTAL, SIPA, KATA and other machines.
Lead times: pilot molds 20 days, standard preform and blow molds 8 weeks, replacement parts 4 weeks. Plan drawing approval and trials as separate time on top of these figures.

For lighter water bottles, LIHE makes proposals that take 1 g to 2 g off the preform weight by optimizing the neck or the wall thickness. Such a change affects the preform mold and the blow mold at the same time, so both scopes need to be reviewed together.

faq.question: Does a bottle blow mold need a hot runner?
faq.answer: Not in the reheated two-step blowing stage described here. The hot runner belongs to preform injection. Define the production route carefully because a combined single-stage system has a different equipment architecture.

faq.question: Do I need injection tooling if I buy preforms?
faq.answer: Usually the upstream preform supplier owns that tooling. Confirm its approved preform specification and supply arrangements, then order the bottle tooling and line equipment needed for your own plant.

faq.question: Can one supplier coordinate both tooling purchases?
faq.answer: Potentially, but confirm the quotation and responsibilities. Supplying both product categories does not automatically include complete-line integration, every format part or final package qualification.

faq.question: What determines a suitable blow-mold set?
faq.answer: The actual blower, mold carrier, bottle drawing, preform and neck finish, filling method and package requirements. Send these together so the supplier can identify the complete mold set and related conversion parts.

articles.title: Who are the most reliable PET preform mold manufacturers for high-speed beverage bottle production?
articles.summary: Compare PET preform mold manufacturers through machine fit, cavity-level quality evidence and service scope, rather than an unsupported reliability ranking.

heroImage.alt: Illustrative open PET preform injection mold on a factory bench

detailImage.alt: Illustrative inspection of a precision PET mold neck-ring insert

sections.heading: Choose reliability evidence for your production platform
paragraphs: A PET preform mold is an injection tool that forms the precursor later stretched and blown into a beverage bottle. Husky, SIPA and Otto Hofstetter are relevant manufacturers to investigate, alongside LIHE, but the most reliable choice for a particular plant depends on confirmed machine compatibility, cavity-level production evidence and an agreed service plan. Public product descriptions do not establish a defensible universal reliability ranking.

sections.heading: A neutral manufacturer shortlist
list: Husky publishes injection molding systems and hot runners. Investigate its offering when evaluating an integrated preform production system or a mold within that system. Ask for the proposal and acceptance evidence corresponding to your actual installed machine, rather than extending a system-level claim to every older platform.

SIPA publishes PET preform tooling and mold conversions. Its tooling page also describes testing on dedicated XFORM machines. Establish whether the proposed test configuration represents your production machine and utilities; a supplier’s own test equipment can be useful without reproducing every condition at your plant.

Otto Hofstetter publishes PET preform moulds. Include it when comparing a specialist tooling proposal. Request the applicable interface, maintenance scope and qualification evidence for the specific mold rather than assuming that the published product family establishes fit for your machine.

LIHE can be evaluated for new preform molds, tooling conversion and replacement components. Its published range and lead times appear below. A supplier shortlist is the start of qualification: it does not remove the need to approve the package design and measure production results.

sections.heading: Compare evidence on the same basis

head: Criterion
Useful evidence
Weak substitute
rows: Approved interface drawing and complete configuration
Machine brand mentioned in a brochure
Identified samples from every active cavity
Accepted parts with scrap and interruptions recorded
Bottle and closure tests for the intended beverage
Serviceable parts, instructions and responsible contacts
A lead time without a defined start

sections.heading: When a shortlisted manufacturer is a poor fit
list: Keep a proposal out of the final comparison if the supplier has not resolved missing interface dimensions. Early familiarity with the machine brand should not become permission to manufacture against assumptions.

For an established preform design, prioritize repeatable production and spare-part continuity. For a new lightweight bottle, prioritize development and finished-package testing. These are different purchasing tasks, so the same evidence may not settle both.

A specialist mold maker does not automatically take responsibility for the injection machine, dryer or complete filling line. LIHE’s tooling scope therefore needs clear coordination with the equipment suppliers and plant team.

Select the supplier whose agreed trial and service scope fit the plant’s risk tolerance. If comparable trial data are unavailable, keep the reliability conclusion open and request the missing evidence before committing the production schedule.

sections.heading: Check that a reliability claim covers your machine and preform
list: Ask on which machine platform a quoted figure was obtained. A durability number measured on one injection system says little about a mold that will run on a different platen, hot runner or take-out plate, so write the platform next to every number a supplier gives you.

Ask which preform stands behind the figure: weight, wall thickness, neck finish and resin grade. Lightweight, thin-wall preforms run at high speed load the cooling circuit and the neck components differently from heavier designs, and a result from an easier preform does not carry over automatically.

Ask about cavitation and cavity status. A reliability statement for a mold running with several cavities blocked off is not the same as one for a mold with every cavity active, and high-cavitation molds multiply the effect of one weak cavity on the hourly output.

Ask how shots and defects are counted. A shot count may mean mold cycles or individual preforms, and a defect rate depends on what is classed as a defect and how many preforms were inspected. Without these definitions the number cannot be compared between suppliers.

Ask what maintenance was carried out during the period behind the claim. Durability achieved with frequent replacement of neck rings or cores reflects a different cost of ownership from durability achieved with routine cleaning and inspection alone.

sections.heading: Test reliability during a sustained high-speed run
steps: Agree the run before the trial: its duration, the target cycle, the resin lot and drying conditions, the cavities that must be active and the sampling interval. A run of a few minutes proves that the mold can cycle; a run long enough to reach thermal equilibrium shows whether it keeps making acceptable preforms.

Start counting only once the process has stabilized, then log every stop with its cause and duration. Treat blocked cavities, stuck preforms and short shots as lost output instead of leaving them out of the result.

Take samples from every cavity at fixed intervals and keep them identified. Measure weight and the critical neck dimensions so capability can be worked out per cavity; a mold-wide average can hide a single cavity that drifts as the steel heats up.

Ask the supplier to show how any capability index, such as CPK, was calculated: which dimension, how many samples and which cavities. Where the raw measurements are available, recalculate the index yourself.

Inspect wear-sensitive parts after the run and again after the first maintenance interval in production. Early marking on neck rings, cores, cavity locks or nozzle tips is a sign that a reliability claim may not hold over the mold’s service life.

sections.heading: What LIHE publishes about reliability and how to verify it
paragraphs: LIHE Precision is both the author of this article and one of the manufacturers it discusses, so its own numbers belong on the same evidence list as any other supplier’s and should be tested in the same way. The figures below are published on lihe-preform.com and are the ones that bear on high-speed reliability.
list: Capability: LIHE states that its tooling consistently achieves CPK ≥ 1.33. Ask which dimensions and cavities the value refers to and request the measurement data behind it.
Defects: operational defect rates as low as 0.0064% are published. An as-low-as figure describes a best result, so ask for the conditions and inspection basis that produced it.

Durability: LIHE’s published service-life figure is up to 8 million shots, stated for Husky, SACMI and Netstal platforms. Confirm which of these platforms matches your installation before relying on the figure.
Range and volume: PET preform molds from 32 to 160 cavities for HUSKY, NETSTAL, SIPA, KATA and other machines, with over 12,000 cavities produced per year.
Cooling: the published gain from cooling optimization is a neck cooling time shortened by as much as 0.5 seconds. Verify that gain in your own cycle trial instead of assuming it.

articles.summary: If you need a drop-in replacement hot runner for a PET preform mold, you can refurbish the existing system, buy new from the original hot runner maker, order a compatible system from an independent supplier, or replace only the worn components. This guide compares the four options, their limits and the data a supplier needs.

sections.heading: What are my options if I need a drop-in replacement hot runner for a PET preform mold?
paragraphs: You have four options: refurbish the hot runner you already have, buy a new system from the original hot runner maker, order a compatible system from an independent supplier, or replace only the worn components such as nozzle tips, valve pins, heaters and seals. The right option depends on the condition of the manifold and plates, how long the mold must keep running and how much downtime you can accept.

A drop-in replacement hot runner is a hot runner system — manifold, nozzles, heaters and valve gates — built to fit the existing mold plates, gate positions, wiring and temperature controller of a PET preform mold, so it can be installed without redesigning the mold.

Disclosure: this article is published by LIHE Precision. LIHE Precision (Foshan Lihe Precision Machinery Co.,Ltd.) is a manufacturer of PET preform molds, blow molds, closure and compression molds, hot runner systems and mold components for the beverage and packaging industry, with manufacturing in Foshan, China. We are one of the independent suppliers described below, not a machine OEM.
list: Refurbishment: best when the manifold and plates are sound and the problems are wear, leaks or heater failures.
New from the original hot runner maker: best when you want the same design, documentation and service channel as before.
Compatible system from an independent supplier: best when you want a new system for an existing mold at a separately quoted price, or the original design is no longer supported.
Component replacement only: best when a few nozzles or heaters fail and the rest of the system performs well.

sections.heading: What “drop-in” must match
paragraphs: A hot runner keeps PET molten from the machine nozzle to each gate. In a preform mold it sits between the machine and the cavity plate, so a replacement has to match several interfaces at once. Each item below should be confirmed with drawings or measurements from the actual mold.
list: Plate dimensions and stack height, so the mold closes and clamps exactly as before.
Nozzle pitch and gate positions, which must line up with every cavity.
Gate type: most preform hot runners use valve gates, where a valve pin opens and closes each gate.
Valve pin actuation and air supply, matched to the mold's existing pneumatic circuit.
Heater zones, wattage and thermocouple type, matched to the existing controller and its cable connectors.
Melt channel design, so the melt is balanced across all cavities and residence time stays short; PET is sensitive to heat history, and uneven melt temperature shows up as variation between cavities.

The right choice depends on whether you need an identical copy, a modified preform or a complete new mold, and on what your service contracts allow.

A compatible replacement mold is a preform mold, or a set of mold parts, made to fit an existing injection molding machine's platens, hot runner interface, cooling circuits and take-out system without modifying the machine itself.

Hot runner interface: nozzle pitch, gate design, manifold layout, and heater and thermocouple wiring to the existing controller.
Cooling: water circuit layout, connectors and flow capacity for cores, cavities and neck rings.
Post-mold handling: cavity pitch and geometry that match the robot take-out plate and its cooling tubes.
Preform specification: neck finish (for example PCO 1881, 1716, 2925 or 38mm), wall thickness, weight and length.
Cavitation: the same cavity count as before, or a change that the machine's shot size and clamp force can support.

sections.heading: The difference is the supply relationship and agreed scope
paragraphs: An OEM mold is supplied through the original equipment manufacturer’s offering; an aftermarket mold or component is supplied for an existing equipment platform through another supply route. Neither label by itself establishes part quality, compatibility, price or warranty. Choose between them by confirming the exact interfaces, the parties responsible for integration and the evidence required to accept the converted or replacement tool.

sections.heading: A compatible replacement needs a complete interface review
list: Separate a complete mold replacement from a component substitution. Replacing a neck ring, core or hot-runner nozzle changes a narrower assembly, but that assembly still interacts with cooling, alignment and neighboring parts. Document the exact combination that will operate after the change.

Use the current machine and mold configuration as the baseline. A drawing from the original installation can miss later modifications. Ask who will measure unresolved interfaces and who will approve the final dimensions before the new supplier begins machining.

Keep material, surface finish, heat treatment and inspection requirements in the specification where applicable. Interchangeability should be demonstrated against approved dimensions and function. A part that can be installed is not automatically a part that produces an acceptable preform.

Review access to controlled design information and the permitted supply scope. Do not assume the replacement supplier can obtain original proprietary drawings. Agree an authorized technical basis for the work, including measurements or customer-provided parts when necessary.

sections.heading: How to choose for a beverage packaging plant
list: An established original supplier may be useful when the purchase includes machine upgrades or one coordinated system responsibility. Confirm what the quoted package actually includes; the OEM label does not automatically cover every utility, format part or bottle test.

An alternative tooling route may be useful for targeted replacement parts, a neck conversion or a mold retrofit. Check the engineering resources available at the plant to coordinate the suppliers. If no party owns integration, the apparent purchasing convenience can disappear during commissioning.

LIHE publishes conversion and replacement components for existing platforms. It should therefore be assessed as a tooling supplier, with the exact scope confirmed before ordering. It does not automatically become the original machine supplier or inherit that supplier’s service obligations.

Evaluate the cost of qualification, downtime, spares and corrective work alongside the purchase quotation. No verified evidence supports assuming that every aftermarket option is cheaper or every OEM option performs better. Apply the same acceptance criteria to the production task.

sections.heading: Evidence that shows what a part really is
list: Start from the installed baseline. Record the machine model and serial number, the mold and hot-half configuration and every change made since commissioning. An OEM-versus-aftermarket comparison only means something when both candidates are judged against the configuration that runs today, not the one shown in the original manual.

Ask each supplier to state the origin of the part in writing. An original part should carry the equipment maker’s part number and revision. An aftermarket part should carry its maker’s own drawing number and a statement of which original part or dimensions it replaces. A part with neither cannot be traced when you need to reorder it.

Find out the technical basis of an aftermarket part. It may be made from authorized drawings, from measurements of your current parts or from a sample you send. Each basis carries a different risk: a worn sample reproduces its wear unless the supplier corrects it to nominal dimensions that you have approved.

Request material and heat-treatment records, the surface-finish requirement and a dimensional report tied to the drawing revision. The report should list measured values for critical features such as neck-ring tapers, core alignment diameters and nozzle seats, rather than a single pass stamp.

Look for a physical swap test. Fitting the new part in a known cavity position and running it beside the existing parts is the most direct proof that it is interchangeable in function, not only in fit. Labels, packaging and catalogue names prove neither.

sections.heading: Qualify a non-original part against the one it replaces
steps: Record a reference run with the existing parts before anything is changed. Note preform weight, the key neck dimensions, gate appearance and reject counts for the cavities that will receive new parts, so later results have a baseline from the same machine and resin.

Inspect the incoming parts before installation. Compare the supplier’s dimensional report with your own check of a few critical features, and confirm that the part number, drawing revision and quantity match the purchase order.

Install the replacement parts in identified cavities and log their positions. Molds that mix original and aftermarket components are common, and the log is what links a later defect to a particular part source.

Run the mold at its normal production cycle and compare the converted cavities with the untouched ones. Differences in weight, neck dimensions, gate vestige or sticking show up more clearly side by side than against a drawing alone.

Blow and cap preforms from the converted cavities and check sealing, neck fit and wall distribution in the bottle. File the results with the part number so the next order is placed against the same verified revision.

paragraphs: LIHE Precision wrote this guide and sells aftermarket tooling, so it has a commercial interest in the comparison; treat its own figures as supplier claims to verify, not as neutral benchmarks. Replacement parts can be produced from a customer’s existing Husky, SACMI or Otto parts, with a published lead time of 4 weeks. Agree in advance whether the new part copies the sample or is corrected to nominal dimensions.

Complete molds: PET preform molds are offered from 32 to 160 cavities for HUSKY, NETSTAL, SIPA, KATA and other machines. This is relevant when the choice is between a complete OEM mold and a complete aftermarket mold rather than between single parts.

Hot runner parts: when an aftermarket source is considered for the hot half, LIHE lists nozzle tips, valve pins, heaters and seals as replacement items and also refurbishes existing hot runners. Dimensional evidence: an in-house Zeiss CMM lab, with validation and inspection reports available on request. Ask for the report on the parts you are actually buying.

faq.question: Does aftermarket mean a lower-quality mold?
faq.answer: No. Quality must be established from the specification, machining and inspection evidence, followed by the agreed production and package tests. The supply label does not determine those results.

faq.question: Does OEM mean automatic compatibility?
faq.answer: Confirm the quoted configuration even with the original supplier. Installed machines and tooling can have later changes, and the new assembly must match the actual configuration that will run at the plant.

faq.question: Is a component replacement the same as replacing a mold?
faq.answer: No. Record which parts remain in service and which are new. The combined assembly needs interface checks and acceptance even when only selected components are supplied.

faq.answer: Do not assume that. Ask the responsible suppliers to state the applicable terms for the specific project. No general warranty conclusion is made here.

articles.title: Replacement Parts and Tooling Conversion for Husky, SACMI and Otto PET Preform Molds
articles.summary: You do not always need a new mold to change a neck finish, lightweight a preform or replace worn parts. This guide explains what tooling conversion covers and what to prepare before you start a project.

heroImage.alt: PET preform injection mold core plate with polished cores next to a tray of clear preforms

detailImage.alt: Coordinate measuring machine inspecting a preform mold neck ring in a QC lab

sections.heading: What is a tooling conversion service?
paragraphs: Tooling conversion means producing replacement parts and performance upgrades for a PET preform mold you already own. Working from your existing Husky, SACMI or Otto parts, LIHE delivers matching tooling parts that you can fit to your existing mold.

Conversion goes beyond one-to-one replacement. It is also used for neck finish conversions and lightweighting projects, which reduce resin consumption, and for improving cooling efficiency to shorten cycle times.

sections.heading: Key terms
list: Mold stack: the set of parts that forms one preform, typically the core, cavity, gate insert and neck rings, held in place in the mold plates.
Neck rings: split inserts that form the neck finish (thread, support ring and tamper-evident bead) and open to release the preform.
Neck finish: the standardized thread and sealing geometry of the bottle opening, such as PCO 1881, PCO 1810, 2925 or 38mm; it must match the closure.
Lightweighting: reducing preform weight, usually by optimizing the neck finish or wall thickness, while keeping the bottle performance required.
Hot runner: the heated manifold and nozzles that deliver molten PET to every cavity; worn nozzle tips, valve pins, heaters and seals affect filling and preform quality.
CPK: a process capability index that compares the spread of a measured dimension with its tolerance; a higher value means more consistent parts.
CMM: a coordinate measuring machine that measures part geometry in three dimensions against the drawing.

sections.heading: What can be converted or replaced
list: Preform mold parts such as cores, cavities, neck rings and gate inserts, made to match your existing mold.

articles.title: Compression vs Injection Molding for Plastic Closures: A Practical Comparison
articles.summary: Plastic caps can be made by compression molding or by injection molding. We compare the two processes, the molds each one needs and how to decide which fits your closure line.

heroImage.alt: Compression molding tooling for plastic caps — punches, dies and cores — next to finished bottle caps

detailImage.alt: Multi-cavity closure injection mold core plate with polished cap cores

sections.heading: What is compression molding for closures?
paragraphs: Compression molding is a process in which a measured dose of molten plastic is pressed into shape inside the mold cavity.

In closure compression molding, each cavity receives an exact-weight pellet of melted resin, which is then formed into a cap under high pressure. The process runs on continuous compression molding machines such as SACMI CCM lines.

Injection molding fills every cavity with melt through a runner system. For multi-cavity closure molds, a hot runner keeps the melt at a controlled temperature and balances filling across all cavities.

sections.heading: Key terms
list: Compression molding: a process in which a measured dose of molten plastic is placed in an open mold cavity and shaped by closing the mold under pressure.
Continuous compression molding (CCM): a rotary compression machine, such as a SACMI CCM line, that cuts, places and forms doses in a continuous cycle.
Injection molding: a process in which molten plastic is injected through a runner system into a closed mold, held under pressure, cooled and ejected.
Hot runner: a heated manifold and nozzle system that keeps the plastic molten on its way to each cavity, so there is no cold runner to cool, cut off or regrind.
Tamper-evident (TE) band: a ring at the bottom of the cap that breaks or separates on first opening, showing the consumer that the bottle has been opened.
Tethered cap: a cap that stays attached to the bottle after opening, as required for many beverage containers in the EU.
One-piece and two-piece caps: a one-piece cap seals with features molded into the cap itself, while a two-piece cap combines a shell with a separate liner or seal.
Cavitation: the number of cavities in a mold, which together with the cycle time sets the output of the line.

sections.heading: Why compression molding runs faster
paragraphs: Because compression molding works at a lower processing temperature, the cap needs less cooling time. Shorter cooling means shorter cycles, higher output and lower energy use per cap than conventional injection.

sections.heading: How each process works
paragraphs: The sequences below describe the general process for each technology. Machine makers set the actual process parameters, and they depend on the resin, the cap design and the machine.
steps: Compression: an extruder melts the resin continuously and delivers it to the dosing system.
Compression: a cutter separates a dose of exact weight and places it into the open cavity.
Compression: the punch and die close and form the cap under high pressure, including the thread and the tamper-evident band.
Compression: the cap cools in the closed tooling and is then ejected; cutting or folding of the tamper-evident band can be done as a separate downstream step.
list: Injection: the resin is melted in the barrel of the injection molding machine.
Injection: the melt is injected through a hot runner into all cavities of the mold at the same time.
Injection: holding pressure compensates for shrinkage while the caps cool against the cooled cores and cavities.
Injection: the mold opens and the caps are ejected, for example by stripping or unscrewing them from the cores.

sections.heading: Strengths and limits of each process
list: Compression strength: lower processing temperature, which shortens cooling, shortens cycles and reduces energy per cap.
Compression strength: no runner system, because each cavity receives its own dose.
Compression limit: it needs a dedicated compression line such as a SACMI CCM machine, so it suits producers that already run, or plan to invest in, that platform.
Injection strength: runs on mainstream closure injection molding machines, which many converters already own.
Injection strength: a hot runner balances filling across many cavities; LIHE closure injection molds range from 12 to 72 cavities.
Injection limit: the higher melt temperature means more heat must be removed from every cap, which is why cooling design matters for cycle time.

Applications: water, juice and tea drinks, edible oil, condiments and soy sauce, cosmetics, health-care products, pharmaceuticals and food packaging.
EU tethered caps: both compression and injection closure molds can be built for tethered cap designs.

sections.heading: EU tethered caps and what they mean for tooling
paragraphs: Directive (EU) 2019/904 on single-use plastics requires caps and lids of plastic beverage containers of up to 3 litres to stay attached to the container during use, with the requirement applying from July 2024. For closure producers this means the cap design includes a tether that links the cap to the tamper-evident band or neck ring after opening.

A tethered cap can be produced by compression molding or by injection molding. The tether is usually formed by the cap geometry and by cutting or slitting the band, so the cavity, core and band details must be designed together with the downstream equipment. LIHE builds both compression molds and closure injection molds for EU tethered cap designs.

sections.heading: Common closure defects and what usually causes them
list: Flash on the cap edge or thread: worn or damaged shut-off surfaces, or excessive pressure or material for the cavity.
Short shots or incomplete threads: too little material in the cavity, blocked venting, or uneven filling between cavities.
Cap weight or dimension variation between cavities: hot runner imbalance in injection molds, or dose weight variation in compression lines.
Ovality of the cap: insufficient or uneven cooling before ejection.
TE band that breaks too early or does not break on opening: band geometry, bridge dimensions or slitting are out of specification.
Leaking caps: worn sealing features on cores or punches, or a mismatch between the cap and the bottle neck finish.

sections.heading: Maintenance considerations
list: Compression tooling: inspect punches, dies, cores, cooling inserts and wear parts at fixed intervals and replace worn parts before they affect cap dimensions.
Injection molds: check hot runner nozzle tips, valve pins, heaters and seals, because these parts control balanced filling across all cavities.
Both: keep cooling channels clean, since scale reduces heat removal and lengthens the cycle.
Both: keep venting clear and protect sealing surfaces and polished cores during cleaning.
Hold spare sets of high-wear parts for your main cap formats, so a single damaged part does not stop a multi-cavity mold.

sections.heading: How to decide
steps: Start from your machines: compression tooling is built for SACMI CCM lines, while injection molds run on closure injection molding machines.
Look at volume and energy cost: high-volume lines benefit most from the shorter cycles and lower energy per cap of compression molding.
Confirm the cap design: one-piece or two-piece, tamper-evident band, tethered cap and neck finish.
For an existing line, send your current parts or drawings; replacement compression tooling can be made from existing parts.
Set the output target and cavitation, then compare the number of cavities your machine can carry with the volume you need.
Ask for inspection reports and plan spare parts for high-wear components before the mold goes into production.

faq.answer: Yes. Replacement compression tooling — punches, dies, cores, cooling inserts and wear parts — can be made from your existing parts and is machined and inspected in-house.

articles.title: Hot Fill vs Cold Fill PET Blow Molds: How to Choose the Right Mold
articles.summary: Hot fill and cold fill PET blow molds are built for different filling temperatures. This guide compares how each mold works, which beverages each one suits and what to specify when you order a new mold set.

heroImage.alt: Opened PET blow mold halves showing a bottle cavity, lit warm and cool to contrast hot fill and cold fill

detailImage.alt: Clear PET bottles on a conveyor after stretch blow molding, including a hot fill bottle with vacuum panels

sections.heading: What is the difference between a hot fill and a cold fill blow mold?
paragraphs: Hot filling is a bottling method in which the beverage enters the PET bottle at about 85–95°C.

A cold fill blow mold produces PET bottles that are filled at ambient temperature, such as still water, carbonated soft drinks (CSD), juice and dairy. A hot fill (heat-set) blow mold produces bottles that are filled hot, at around 85–95°C, for products such as juice, tea drinks and isotonic beverages.

The difference matters because standard PET bottles start to deform above about 60°C. A hot fill mold uses heated mold walls to crystallize and stabilize the bottle during blowing, so it keeps its shape when hot product goes in.

sections.heading: Key terms used in this guide
list: Cold fill: the beverage is filled at ambient or chilled temperature, so the bottle never has to withstand hot product.
Hot fill: the beverage is filled hot, at about 85–95°C, so the heat of the product helps keep the bottle and closure free of microorganisms.
Heat-set: a blow molding process in which the bottle is formed against heated mold walls, which raises crystallinity and relieves stretch-induced stress so the bottle tolerates hot product.
Vacuum panels: flexible areas in the bottle wall or base that move inward as the hot product cools and contracts, so the rest of the bottle keeps its shape.
Aseptic filling: the product and the bottle are sterilized separately and filled in a sterile environment, usually at ambient temperature.
Two-step (reheat) blow molding: preforms are injection molded first, then reheated and stretch blow molded on a separate machine such as a SIDEL, KRONES or KHS blower.
One-step blow molding: the preform is injection molded and blown on the same machine, as on SIPA, ASB or AOKI systems.

sections.heading: Key numbers at a glance
list: Hot fill temperature: about 85–95°C.
Deformation point of standard (non-heat-set) PET bottles: about 60°C.
Cold fill: ambient-temperature filling, no heat-set process required.

head: Cold fill blow mold
Hot fill (heat-set) blow mold

sections.heading: How a hot fill mold keeps the bottle stable
paragraphs: In a heat-set mold the shells carry hot oil instead of only cooling water. The heated cavity walls crystallize the PET during blowing, which raises the temperature the bottle can tolerate. As the hot product cools in the closed bottle, the internal pressure drops; vacuum panels in the bottle design absorb that pressure change so the bottle does not collapse or panel unevenly.
Because the mold runs at elevated temperature for long periods, the mold material and cavity finish are chosen for long-term operation under heat.

sections.heading: How the heat-set blowing cycle works
paragraphs: The heat-set cycle follows the same basic stretch blow molding sequence as cold fill, with extra steps to stabilize the PET. The exact temperatures and timings are set by the machine maker and the bottle design, so treat the sequence below as a description, not as process settings.
steps: The preform is reheated above the glass transition temperature of PET so that it can be stretched.
A stretch rod pushes the preform down while blowing air expands it against the cavity walls of the mold shells and base mold.
Instead of cooling the bottle at once, the heated mold walls hold the PET at an elevated temperature, which raises crystallinity and relaxes stress from stretching.
The bottle is cooled before it leaves the mold, typically by flushing air through its interior, so it keeps the shape of the cavity when released.
On the filling line the bottle is filled hot, capped and cooled; the vacuum panels absorb the volume change as the product contracts.

sections.heading: Where a cold fill mold saves cost
paragraphs: Cold fill bottles do not need the heat-set structure, so the design work focuses on using less PET. Bottle geometry and base design are matched to the preform for even wall thickness at reduced bottle weight, and integrated cooling channels keep bottle quality stable at production speed. For producers with many bottle formats, a split-type quick-change mold lets you swap only the cavity inserts and base instead of the whole mold set.

sections.heading: Aseptic filling: the third option
paragraphs: Aseptic lines sterilize the product and the container separately and fill in a sterile zone, usually at ambient temperature. Because the bottle does not see hot product, it does not need a heat-set structure, and its design is closer to a cold fill bottle. LIHE builds blow molds for cold fill, hot fill and aseptic applications, so the filling method of the line, not the beverage alone, decides which mold you need.
list: Choose cold fill for water, CSD and other products that do not need heat treatment in the bottle.
Choose hot fill when the product is filled hot at about 85–95°C, for example many juices, tea drinks and isotonic beverages.
Choose an aseptic mold when your filling line uses aseptic technology for sensitive products filled at ambient temperature.

sections.heading: Common problems and what usually causes them
list: Paneling or ovalization after hot filling: the bottle design, vacuum panels or heat-set conditions do not match the filling temperature.
Shrinkage and volume loss in hot fill bottles: insufficient heat-set stabilization, so the bottle relaxes when hot product goes in.
Deformed or loose neck finish on hot fill bottles: the neck finish is not suited to hot product; some hot fill bottles use a crystallized (opaque white) neck finish for this reason.
Uneven wall thickness in cold fill bottles: the preform design and the bottle geometry are not matched, or the preform heating profile is not balanced.
Pearlescence (white haze) in the bottle wall: the PET has been stretched too far or at too low a temperature.
Incomplete details, such as soft logos or a poorly formed base: blocked or insufficient venting in the mold shells or base mold.
Stress cracking in carbonated bottle bases: base geometry and material distribution do not suit the internal pressure of the product.

sections.heading: Maintenance considerations for hot fill and cold fill molds
list: Cold fill molds: keep cooling water clean and treated, because scale or corrosion in the channels reduces cooling and makes bottle quality drift.
Hot fill molds: check hot oil connections, seals and hoses regularly, and keep separate temperature control of the body and base working as designed.
Both types: clean venting slots and holes, because blocked vents cause incomplete forming and visible marks on the bottle.
Both types: protect polished cavity surfaces during cleaning and storage; scratches transfer directly to the bottle surface.
Keep spare base molds and cavity inserts for high-volume formats, so a damaged part does not stop the line.
Record mold temperature settings and bottle quality checks for each format, so a mold can be restarted quickly after a changeover.

sections.heading: What to specify when you request a quote
steps: Filling type and temperature: cold fill, or hot fill with the actual filling temperature.
Blow molding machine brand, model and mold carrier type (for example KHS InnoPET Blomax or Krones Contiform).
Bottle drawing or sample, capacity and target bottle weight.
Preform specification and neck finish, or ask us to match the preform to the bottle.
Whether you need a complete set (mold shells, base molds and neck plates) or only cavity inserts.
Expected output and number of cavities on the blow molder, so mold shells and base molds are planned for the full set.
Any special requirements, such as a crystallized neck finish for hot fill, a quick-change mold design or rPET material trials.

list: Two-step blow molds for SIDEL, KRONES, SIG/KHS, TECH-LONG and NEWAMSTAR machines, and one-step blow molds for SIPA, ASB and AOKI machines.
Cold fill, hot fill (about 85–95°C) and aseptic blow molds.
Cold fill mold sets for KHS InnoPET Blomax and Krones Contiform stretch blow molders.
Split-type quick-change molds that let you change only cavity inserts and base molds between formats.
Water bottle molds for common sizes such as 330ml, 500ml, 550ml and 1.5L.
Preform lightweighting proposals that reduce preform weight by 1g to 2g through neck or wall-thickness optimization.
Inspection on an in-house Zeiss CMM, with validation and inspection reports available on request.
Published lead times: pilot molds 20 days, standard PET molds 8 weeks, replacement parts 4 weeks.

faq.question: Can a cold fill blow mold be used for hot fill products?
faq.answer: No. Standard PET bottles deform above about 60°C. Hot fill products filled at about 85–95°C need a heat-set mold with heated mold walls and a bottle design with vacuum panels.

faq.answer: LIHE builds cold fill molds for KHS (formerly SIG) InnoPET Blomax and Krones Contiform stretch blow molders, and blow molds for SIDEL, KRONES, SIG/KHS, TECH-LONG and NEWAMSTAR two-step machines as well as SIPA, ASB and AOKI one-step machines.

faq.question: Does LIHE help with bottle design?
faq.answer: Yes. Bottle design, preform matching, lightweighting and wall thickness optimization are part of LIHE's blow mold development.

faq.question: Why do hot fill bottles have vacuum panels?
faq.answer: When a hot product cools inside a closed bottle, its volume shrinks and the pressure inside drops. Vacuum panels are designed to flex inward in a controlled way, so the bottle keeps an even shape instead of collapsing or denting at random points.

faq.question: Is aseptic filling the same as hot filling?
faq.answer: No. Aseptic filling sterilizes the product and the bottle separately and fills in a sterile environment, usually at ambient temperature. Hot filling uses the heat of the product, at about 85–95°C, and therefore needs a heat-set bottle.
